title: Website redesign on a fixed launch date
description: Your team is rebuilding the company marketing website for a launch date fixed by an advertising campaign. Keep schedule, budget, quality and morale healthy through four weeks of surprises.
assumptions: Team of six: two designers, three developers and one content lead, full-time on this project.
The launch date is fixed by a marketing campaign; scope is flexible, the date is not.
Measures are health scores from 0 (critical) to 100 (excellent), not literal percentages.
Effects of decisions are simplified training models, not statistical forecasts.
Every measure slowly erodes each day as ordinary project pressure; good decisions offset it.

events.title: Stakeholder wants five extra pages
events.description: Marketing has just asked for five extra landing pages 'while you're at it'.

events.title: Lead developer out sick for a week
events.description: Your lead developer is unwell and will be out for the next week.

events.title: Client content arrives a week late
events.description: The copy and images promised for content freeze have not arrived.

events.title: Critical browser bug found
events.description: Testing shows the checkout form breaks on a popular browser, five days before beta.

events.title: Stakeholders love the early build
events.description: A preview demo gets warm feedback from senior stakeholders.

events.title: Finance asks for 10% cuts
events.description: Finance has asked every project to return 10% of its remaining budget.

events.title: Hosting migration goes smoothly
events.description: The move to the new hosting platform finishes without incident.

decisions.prompt: Marketing wants five extra landing pages. How do you respond?

options.label: Accept all five pages
options.tradeoff: Keeps marketing happy, but adds a lot of work to an already tight plan.

options.label: Add two now, three after launch
options.tradeoff: A compromise that limits the damage but needs some negotiation effort.

options.label: Decline: scope is frozen
options.tradeoff: Protects the plan, but creates friction that the team has to absorb.

decisions.prompt: Your lead developer is out for a week. What do you do?

options.label: Ask the team to work overtime
options.tradeoff: Recovers time, but tired people make mistakes and burn out.

options.label: Bring in a contractor
options.tradeoff: Fast and effective, but expensive and needs onboarding.

options.label: Cut low-priority features
options.tradeoff: Keeps the team sane, but the product gets thinner.

decisions.prompt: The client content is a week late. How do you proceed?

options.label: Build with placeholder content
options.tradeoff: Development continues, but real content may not fit the layouts.

options.label: Escalate to the client sponsor
options.tradeoff: Gets the content moving, at the cost of some goodwill and stress.

options.label: Have the team write it
options.tradeoff: Unblocks everything, but it is not the team's strength and takes effort.

decisions.prompt: A critical browser bug was found five days before beta. What now?

options.label: Stop and fix it properly
options.tradeoff: The right fix, but it costs time and money right now.

options.label: Ship a workaround and fix it later
options.tradeoff: Keeps the date, but leaves a known weakness in the product.

options.label: Remove the affected feature for launch
options.tradeoff: Removes the risk, but disappoints the people who wanted that feature.

decisions.prompt: Finance wants 10% of the remaining budget back. What do you cut?

options.label: Cut testing time
options.tradeoff: Easiest saving, but you will find fewer problems before users do.

options.label: Cut some scope
options.tradeoff: Saves money and effort, but the site launches with less.

options.label: Present data and push back
options.tradeoff: Protects the plan if it works; costs time to prepare and argue.
